JSON: Name: self_configuring_mplc Title: In-situ transmission-matrix-driven optimisation of multi-plane light converters using high-speed MEMS phase modulators to reduce mode cross-talk and convergence time for high-dimensional spatial mode transformations Short Hypothesis: An in-situ, transmission-matrix-driven iterative optimisation of a multi-plane light converter implemented with a kHz-class MEMS phase-only light modulator will converge to unitary mappings of up to ten orthogonal spatial input modes with mean inter-channel cross-talk ≤ −18 dB and total optimisation time ≤ 10 minutes, outperforming an equivalent offline inverse-design (wavefront-matching) implementation in both cross-talk and convergence time. Related Work: Existing approaches to high-dimensional free-space spatial mode transformation include: (a) inverse-design and adjoint-gradient numerical optimisation of cascaded phase planes (wavefront matching, adjoint-based MPLC design), which produce high-fidelity designs offline but are highly sensitive to model–system mismatch and fabrication/alignment errors; (b) single-plane and single-SLM wavefront-shaping methods and transmission-matrix (TM) measurement techniques that can correct scattering in situ for one or few modes but do not naturally scale to full multi-plane MPLC designs; (c) liquid-crystal SLM-based multi-reflection MPLCs that enable programmable cascades but are limited by slow refresh rates, polarization sensitivity, and pixel crosstalk; (d) photonic integrated circuit implementations which can implement unitary transforms on-chip but face scaling, fabrication complexity, and limited free-space mode interfacing. Limitations across these methods include: requirement for accurate physical models for offline design, cumulative sensitivity to inter-plane misalignment and aberrations, slow reconfiguration times on conventional SLMs, large measurement overheads for TM characterization, and reduced experimental fidelity when model assumptions are violated. Abstract: High-dimensional free-space spatial mode transformations implemented via multi-plane light converters (MPLCs) enable parallel deterministic mapping between orthogonal input and output field bases, but existing offline inverse-design pipelines degrade markedly when the digital model deviates from the physical system and when devices must be reconfigured rapidly. We propose and evaluate a self-configuring MPLC pipeline that treats the optical device itself as the complex medium: it measures transmission matrices in situ and iteratively updates phase planes to absorb unknown misalignments and aberrations into the realised design. The method extends single-plane wavefront-shaping to simultaneous multi-plane, multi-mode optimisation and leverages high-speed phase-only MEMS modulators to explore millions of configurations quickly. The main contribution is a practical optimisation protocol and fast hardware platform that jointly calibrates and configures an MPLC without a priori physical models, delivering high-fidelity arbitrary unitary-like spatial transforms and universal mode sorting. Expected outcomes include reduced dependence on precise alignment, faster convergence compared with offline design workflows, and robust operation under realistic environmental drift, enabling compact, reconfigurable spatial-mode processors for communications, imaging, and photonic computing. Experiments: Datasets: sets of orthogonal spatial mode bases and scrambled fields: (1) Hermite–Gaussian modes up to 10 distinct modes (HG basis N={1..10}), (2) Laguerre–Gaussian modes up to 10 modes (LG basis), (3) ensembles of orthogonal speckle modes with N={3,5,7}, (4) experimentally measured multimode-fibre-scrambled output fields for 5 and 10-channel testcases. Baselines: (A) offline inverse-design MPLC computed by wavefront-matching/adjoint optimisation and implemented physically on the same hardware (model-based), (B) conventional single-reflection liquid-crystal SLM multiplexing (single-plane multiplexed holograms), (C) fixed passive MPLC design (fabricated reference) where available. Evaluation metrics: per-mode fidelity (complex-field overlap |⟨v_target,v_measured⟩|), mean inter-channel cross-talk in dB (average off-diagonal energy fraction → dB), total light-processing efficiency (fraction of input power at intended outputs), convergence time (wall-clock time to reach fidelity threshold, e.g., 0.90), number of TM measurements, and robustness under induced perturbations (mechanical misalignment Δx, angular tilt Δθ, and temperature change ΔT). Experimental setup: Mach–Zehnder interferometric measurement of output complex fields via single-shot off-axis digital holography, iterative TM measurement from each MPLC plane to output with plane-wave or Hadamard sampling P∈{1024,4096,8100}, and phase plane updates using a high-speed MEMS phase-only light modulator operating at variable frame rates f∈{720Hz,1.44kHz,10kHz (projected)}; use M∈{2,4,6} phase planes. Protocol: for each dataset and N, run (i) self-configuring TM-driven optimisation (proposed), (ii) baseline A implemented offline then loaded to device, (iii) baseline B implementation; measure metrics above. Ablations: (1) vary plane count M to quantify M vs fidelity and efficiency; (2) vary sample count P per TM to quantify TM sampling resolution effect; (3) disable inter-TM phase-drift stabilisation to measure sensitivity; (4) vary MEMS frame-rate f to quantify convergence time scaling; (5) test discrete piston depth (4-bit vs higher resolution) to measure quantisation effects. Statistical analysis: report mean ± std over ≥10 independent trials per condition, perform pairwise comparisons (Wilcoxon signed-rank) between proposed method and each baseline for fidelity and convergence time, and report effect size. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: interferometric phase drift between reference and signal arms causing corrupted TM measurements; limited piston bit depth and finite micro-mirror flatness causing quantisation error and residual aberrations; limited PLM reflectivity and fill factor reducing overall efficiency. Measurement and evaluation biases: incomplete capture of scattered/transmitted fields (camera field-of-view), non-uniform sampling of plane-wave basis leading to aliasing, and calibration-dependent metric inflation. Scalability and compute limits: optimisation time and measurement count scale approximately O(P·N·M·C), leading to impractical runtimes for large N unless TM sampling is compressed; holographic reconstruction and mask-update computational bottlenecks may dominate. Generalization limits: wavelength dependence of phase modulation and coatings limits broadband/multicolour operation; method assumes ability to measure complex fields (requires reference beam) and thus may not apply where interferometric reference is infeasible; performance degrades for non-orthogonal or highly overlapping input sets proportional to modal overlap; robustness to extreme environmental perturbations (large mechanical shifts, sudden temperature excursions) is limited by measurement cadence and stabilisation effectiveness. Hardware constraints: availability and maturity of kHz-class MEMS PLMs with sufficient piston depth, mirror flatness, and optical coatings; optical footprint and insertion loss may preclude some compact or power-sensitive applications.
